title: Ground Rules That Promote Open Discussion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article catalogs several practical ground rules leaders can set before a group discussion to encourage candor and reduce inhibition. It walks through the Chatham House Rule (ideas can be used but not attributed), the Rule of Charity (assume good intent), the No Interruption Rule paired with a time limit per speaker, the Inexperienced First Rule (junior voices speak before senior ones anchor the conversation), and the Agree to Disagree Rule for unresolvable differences. The piece frames these as low-cost, high-leverage tools that any leader can announce at the start of a meeting to shape how freely people participate. It closes with a wry nod to the simplest ground rule of all: no cell phones.
points: The Chatham House Rule lets participants use ideas discussed without attributing who said them.
The Rule of Charity asks people to presume good intent, reducing defensiveness in debate.
Pairing a No Interruption Rule with a speaking-time limit keeps discussions efficient and fair.
The Inexperienced First Rule invites junior voices to speak before senior opinions anchor the room.
Stating ground rules up front, especially with unfamiliar groups, makes them far more likely to hold.
quotes: Creating open and candid discussion is never easy, especially in large groups.
The Chatham House Rule allows people to express and discuss controversial opinions without attributing the source.
This rule states that everyone will assume what others say is well-intended.
The adjacent rule of a 90-second-to-three-minute speech duration asks people to be succinct.
Simple rules can materially enhance any discussion or exchange.
